text_en: Yes. Based on the description... Yes, a lot of data is missing. Besides, as I said at the very beginning, I have no idea what this original dataset looked like, if only because I don't know North American mushrooms very well. If there's some pool of species there, and in this set... I understand that species occurring only in North America weren't discarded and only the shared ones chosen, then there could be a whole group of species that don't come to mind but which in reality are common there and are, say, edible or poisonous. So that's the first difficulty. The second is the absence of certain features one looks at — how the stipe surface looks, or the hymenophore type. By default I understand it's gilled, because that's how the dataset was given at the start; and we also know the gills are orange, but it's also hard to say — important from a mycologist's point of view — for example the way the gills attach, right? Whether these gills have some edging or not? That's missing; it's a fairly massive mushroom, so I'm trying to think what else it could be, given it started as inedible or poisonous — maybe some Hypholoma, maybe some Hebeloma (poisonpie); it's hard to say. But absolutely crucial to me — and suspicious — is why solely lengthening the stipe suddenly makes the algorithm change the classification, all the more since we don't quite know how these mushrooms were photographed at the start, and secondly the way fruiting bodies grow sometimes deforms the fruiting body itself — for example ones growing from places with a lot of fallen wood, the stipe pushes through a thick layer to finally form the cap. Then if someone yanks it hard, they pull it out with a terribly long stipe, and it can be quite a distortion. Yes, these are rare cases, but they should be taken into account too, so this set of features, for me as someone who works with mushrooms — European ones at least — is a bit too little to unambiguously classify this fruiting body into any specific systematic group.
